messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Rape
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was sixty-eight years old when he came to his first appointment, though the exhaustion in his face made him look older. He had worked for a nonprofit focused on housing advocacy for nearly two decades, a career he had built carefully after his divorce fifteen years prior. He lived alone in a modest apartment in Queens, had maintained a small circle of professional colleagues, and had settled into what he believed was a manageable life. That was before the night that unmade him.

Three years ago, at sixty-five, Rajesh had stayed late at the office to finish grant applications. It was a Tuesday in March. He left around nine in the evening, taking the subway home as he always did. The attack happened in the stairwell of his apartment building—a man with a knife who forced him into the dark space between the fourth and fifth floors. What followed was a violation so complete and so sudden that Rajesh's mind seemed to fracture under the weight of it. The attacker spoke very little, but the sounds he made—the breathing, the rustle of fabric, a low grunt—became the soundtrack of Rajesh's terror. Afterward, Rajesh made it to his apartment, locked the door, and called the police only after sitting motionless for nearly an hour.

In the weeks that followed, Rajesh noticed he could no longer tolerate being alone. The silence of his apartment, once a refuge after long days at work, became suffocating. He began going to the office earlier and staying later, lingering in the hallways even after everyone had left, unable to face the moment when he would have to drive home and climb those stairs. When he did enter his apartment, he found himself positioning his chair—the one where he ate dinner, where he tried to watch television—so that his back pressed against the wall. From that vantage point, he could see the entire room, the doorway, any potential threat. He could not explain this impulse to himself at first; it simply felt necessary, the way breathing felt necessary.

The sounds haunted him. Every unexpected noise—a car horn, a door slamming in a neighboring unit, the building's pipes settling—sent a jolt through his body that left him shaking. He had begun to listen obsessively for sounds that might indicate someone entering his building, his apartment. At work, where he had once been known for his calm presence and steady judgment during staff meetings, Rajesh found himself tensing at the scrape of a chair, the sudden laugh of a colleague rounding a corner. When his supervisor, Maria, had placed a hand on his shoulder during a tense budget discussion, he had jerked away with such visible alarm that she had stepped back, confused and hurt.

The memories came in fragments that his mind could not quite stitch into language. He knew what had happened—his body knew it acutely—but when he tried to tell the police detective, or later when he attempted to speak to a therapist he saw once and never returned to, the words dissolved. What remained instead were the sounds: that breathing, that grunt, the metallic jingle of a belt buckle. When these auditory echoes returned, often without warning, they arrived alongside a sharp pain in his lower abdomen and a burning sensation in his throat. His body was remembering what his words could not articulate.

Over the months, Rajesh had come to believe that his inability to manage any of this—the hypervigilance, the isolation, the way he flinched at touch, the nights he hurt himself by pressing his fingernails into his palms until they bled, seeking the sharp clarity of physical pain as a way to interrupt the overwhelming internal chaos—all of it proved he was a lousy coper. Other people survived trauma. Other people moved forward. He was stuck, diminished, a man permanently altered into something he no longer recognized. He was certain he would never feel joy or ease or the simple comfort of human contact again. At work, he had become an outsider, a man people approached carefully if at all, sensing something broken in him that they could not name.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was Maria. She had noticed his deterioration and, rather than letting it pass, she had sat with him in his office and said simply that she cared about him and that he deserved support. He had wept—something he had not allowed himself to do since the attack—and had agreed to try again.
